plan.topic_summary: AI agents are systems that autonomously plan, reason, and use tools to accomplish multi-step tasks. For a 1-5 year view, the central question is whether they can operate reliably in production at acceptable cost and safety levels, and how the open vs closed model landscape will shape commercial adoption and competitive structure.
key_questions: What are the current reliability and failure rates for AI agents in production deployments, and what are the primary technical blockers to scaling beyond narrow use cases in the next 12 months?
How are per-task inference costs trending, and at what cost threshold do agents become economically viable for mainstream enterprise workloads within 1-3 years?

How will the open vs closed model landscape affect agent capability and cost over the next 1-3 years, and which architectural approaches (single-agent, multi-agent, hierarchical) are emerging as dominant?
What evaluation frameworks are becoming standard for measuring agent capability, and how well do they correlate with real-world task success rates?

What safety and alignment challenges must be resolved before AI agents can operate with meaningful autonomy in high-stakes domains over the 3-5 year horizon, and what regulatory frameworks are likely to emerge?
Will AI agents displace existing software categories such as RPA and workflow automation, or create entirely new market categories, and what does that imply for competitive structure over 3-5 years?

sources.title: AI Agents That Matter
sources.abstract: AI agents are an exciting new research direction, and agent development is driven by benchmarks. Our analysis of current agent benchmarks and evaluation practices reveals several shortcomings that hinder their usefulness in real-world applications. First, there is a narrow focus on accuracy without attention to other metrics. As a result, SOTA agents are needlessly complex and costly, and the community has reached mistaken conclusions about the sources of accuracy gains. Our focus on cost in addition to accuracy motivates the new goal of jointly optimizing the two metrics. We design and implement one such optimization, showing its potential to greatly reduce cost while maintaining accuracy. Second, the benchmarking needs of model and downstream developers have been conflated, making it hard to identify which agent would be best suited for a particular application. Third, many agent benchmarks have inadequate holdout sets, and sometimes none at all. This has led to agents that are fragile because they take shortcuts and overfit to the benchmark in various ways. We prescribe a principled framework for avoiding overfitting. Finally, there is a lack of standardization in evaluation practices, leading to a pervasive lack of reproducibility. We hope that the steps we introduce for addressing these shortcomings will spur the development of agents that are useful in the real world and not just accurate on benchmarks.

sources.title: A cybersecurity AI agent selection and decision support framework
sources.abstract: This paper presents a novel, structured decision support framework that systematically aligns diverse artificial intelligence (AI) agent architectures, reactive, cognitive, hybrid, and learning, with the comprehensive National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0. By integrating agent theory with industry guidelines, this framework provides a transparent and stepwise methodology for selecting and deploying AI solutions to address contemporary cyber threats. Employing a granular decomposition of NIST CSF 2.0 functions into specific tasks, the study links essential AI agent properties such as autonomy, adaptive learning, and real-time responsiveness to each subcategory's security requirements. In addition, it outlines graduated levels of autonomy (assisted, augmented, and fully autonomous) to accommodate organisations at varying stages of cybersecurity maturity. This holistic approach transcends isolated AI applications, providing a unified detection, incident response, and governance strategy. Through conceptual validation, the framework demonstrates how tailored AI agent deployments can align with real-world constraints and risk profiles, enhancing situational awareness, accelerating response times, and fortifying long-term resilience via adaptive risk management. Ultimately, this research bridges the gap between theoretical AI constructs and operational cybersecurity demands, establishing a foundation for robust, empirically validated multi-agent systems that adhere to industry standards.

sources.title: Visibility into AI Agents
sources.venue: ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT)
sources.abstract: Increased delegation of commercial, scientific, governmental, and personal activities to AI agents—systems capable of pursuing complex goals with limited supervision—may exacerbate existing societal risks and introduce new risks. Understanding and mitigating these risks involves critically evaluating existing governance structures, revising and adapting these structures where needed, and ensuring accountability of key stakeholders. Information about where, why, how, and by whom certain AI agents are used, which we refer to as visibility, is critical to these objectives. In this paper, we assess three categories of measures to increase visibility into AI agents: agent identifiers, real-time monitoring, and activity logging. For each, we outline potential implementations that vary in intrusiveness and informativeness. We analyze how the measures apply across a spectrum of centralized through decentralized deployment contexts, accounting for various actors in the supply chain including hardware and software service providers. Finally, we discuss the implications of our measures for privacy and concentration of power. Further work into understanding the measures and mitigating their negative impacts can help to build a foundation for the governance of AI agents.

sources.title: Safe, Untrusted, "Proof-Carrying" AI Agents: toward the agentic lakehouse
sources.abstract: Data lakehouses run sensitive workloads, where AI-driven automation raises concerns about trust, correctness, and governance. We argue that API-first, programmable lakehouses provide the right abstractions for safe-by-design, agentic workflows. Using Bauplan as a case study, we show how data branching and declarative environments extend naturally to agents, enabling reproducibility and observability while reducing the attack surface. We present a proof-of-concept in which agents repair data pipelines using correctness checks inspired by proof-carrying code. Our prototype demonstrates that untrusted AI agents can operate safely on production data and outlines a path toward a fully agentic lakehouse.

sources.title: AI Agents vs. Agentic AI: A Conceptual taxonomy, applications and challenges
sources.abstract: Information fusion, in the context of the Generative AI era, must distinguish AI Agents from Agentic AI. This review critically distinguishes between AI Agents and Agentic AI, offering a structured, conceptual taxonomy, application mapping, and analysis of opportunities and challenges to clarify their divergent design philosophies and capabilities. We begin by outlining the search strategy and foundational definitions, characterizing AI Agents as modular systems driven and enabled by LLMs and LIMs for task-specific automation. Generative AI is positioned as a precursor providing the foundation, with AI agents advancing through tool integration, prompt engineering, and reasoning enhancements. We then characterize Agentic AI systems, which, in contrast to AI Agents, represent a paradigm shift marked by multi-agent collaboration, dynamic task decomposition, persistent memory, and coordinated autonomy. Through a chronological evaluation of architectural evolution, operational mechanisms, interaction styles, and autonomy levels, we present a comparative analysis across both AI agents and agentic AI paradigms. Application domains enabled by AI Agents such as customer support, scheduling, and data summarization are then contrasted with Agentic AI deployments in research automation, robotic coordination, and medical decision support. We further examine unique challenges in each paradigm including hallucination, brittleness, emergent behavior, and coordination failure, and propose targeted solutions such as ReAct loops, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), automation coordination layers, and causal modeling. This work aims to provide a roadmap for developing robust, scalable, and explainable AI-driven systems.

sources.title: What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation
sources.abstract: Bot detectors deployed at scale treat traffic as binary: human or bot. This assumption breaks when AI agents browse the web through browser automation, a traffic class that is neither and that binary classifiers structurally cannot represent. We present a three-class detection framework distinguishing humans, bots, and AI agents, and show that the binary-vs-agent confusion is architectural: a binary human-vs-bot detector misroutes agent sessions because its label space lacks an agent class. On our controlled benchmark, an MLP binary classifier misclassifies 39.1% of real AI agents as human and a SAINT binary transformer misclassifies 34.5%; adding an explicit agent class yields per-class agent F1 = 1.000 in all 30 runs (3 model families $\times$ 10 seeds). To measure evasion resistance, we construct a five-level evasion ladder spanning passive observation, GAN-generated trajectories, and replay of real human cursor data ($n = 2299$ evasion sessions). Across 10 seeds and 3 model families we observe zero agent misses in 22990 per-seed predictions. The discriminative signal is a browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning: Playwright does not emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams a physical input device produces, and this absence signature survives trajectory manipulation. Exhaustive search over all feature subsets of size 1-5 (9401 GBMs) shows that two behavioral features (mouse_event_rate, teleport_click_ratio) give 100% observed agent recall at every evasion level with agent precision 0.994; five features lift macro-F1 to 0.991. The signal is redundantly encoded: removing teleport_click_ratio leaves agent detection at 100%. The single-feature regime is degenerate, flagging every agent only by collapsing the classifier to always predict "agent". Two features robustly isolate agents; five separate all three traffic classes at macro-F1 $\geq 0.99$.

sources.title: Governing AI Agents
Continuous Process-Level Evaluation for Evolving Enterprise AI Agent Skills
sources.abstract: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, yet final-output evaluation can miss process-level behavioral drift. We present a continuous evaluation framework combining outcome-level and process-level checks, applied to Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system. The framework independently computes per-run ground truth, materializes reusable template tests, and evaluates tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity through programmatic checks and a narrowly scoped LLM judge. We evaluate 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models. Of 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6 percent; Wilson 95 percent CI: 87.7-95.6 percent) contained another evaluator-detected deviation. Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1 percent; 95 percent CI: 86.9-95.3 percent) still violated a trajectory check. Dependency attribution reduced a mean of 6.34 failed checks per run to 2.65 roots. Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with exploratory bootstrap interaction intervals excluding zero for all three Revenue comparisons and one of three Productivity comparisons. Runtime-resolved templates provided reusable regression coverage across the evaluated configurations; longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

sources.title: Empowering biomedical discovery with AI agents
sources.abstract: We envision "AI scientists" as systems capable of skeptical learning and reasoning that empower biomedical research through collaborative agents that integrate AI models and biomedical tools with experimental platforms. Rather than taking humans out of the discovery process, biomedical AI agents combine human creativity and expertise with AI's ability to analyze large datasets, navigate hypothesis spaces, and execute repetitive tasks. AI agents are poised to be proficient in various tasks, planning discovery workflows and performing self-assessment to identify and mitigate gaps in their knowledge. These agents use large language models and generative models to feature structured memory for continual learning and use machine learning tools to incorporate scientific knowledge, biological principles, and theories. AI agents can impact areas ranging from virtual cell simulation, programmable control of phenotypes, and the design of cellular circuits to developing new therapies.

sources.title: Foundations of a Time-Consistent Counterfactual Actuarial Runtime for Autonomous AI Agents
sources.abstract: We propose a foundational runtime actuarial layer for autonomous AI agents in which every side-effect-bearing action carries a time-consistent, counterfactual risk toll computed against a contractually fixed safe default, inside an explicit underwriting boundary. The framework treats per-action insurance as the primary unit of analysis and replaces post-hoc annual liability cover with a pre-action transaction layer. The paper establishes four structural results: (i) a well-defined counterfactual toll under a chosen safe-default mapping and continuation policy, with explicit non-uniqueness; (ii) a no-splitting property within an underwriting boundary that telescopes path-decomposed actions into a boundary potential, with a corollary tying gaming-resistance to boundary design; (iii) an irreversible-authority premium, split into a strictly positive action-level component and an if-and-only-if characterisation of the set-level robust capital increase; and (iv) a conservative runtime gating theorem that translates high-probability toll envelopes into an executed-action budget guarantee. The result is the mathematical base layer for a broader program: an empirical companion instantiates the runtime through an Actuarial Action Interface and authority-frontier experiments; a mechanism-design companion studies strategic operator incentives and cross-boundary aggregation; and a dynamic-underwriting companion studies experience rating and audit-replay calibration. The present paper states the primitive contract, the toll identity, the within-boundary no-arbitrage result, and the budget guarantee on which those later layers depend.

sources.title: Cryptographically verifiable authorization for autonomous AI agents: a falsifiable hypothesis and proof of concept
sources.abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly execute actions, invoke tools, and operate on protected resources with limited human oversight. Existing authentication and authorization mechanisms establish identity and delegate authority but do not inherently provide cryptographic evidence that a concrete request issued by a specific agent satisfies the applicable policy in a specific execution context. This study hypothesizes that agent authorization can be formalized as a cryptographically verifiable relation, denoted $R_{CVA}$, that jointly binds an agent principal, a concrete authorization request, an execution context, and the satisfaction of an applicable policy, while selectively preserving the confidentiality of private authorization attributes. We introduce a preliminary formal abstraction for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA), define a compact set of candidate security properties including authorization soundness, principal binding, request binding, policy binding, and replay resistance, and provide an executable zero-knowledge proof of concept that instantiates selected elements of the model over a Groth16 zk-SNARK construction. We further identify and formalize the structural separation among identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem in the design of secure agentic systems, a distinction to our knowledge, has not been formalized within a cryptographically verifiable authorization relation by current agentic security frameworks, and present a falsifiable research agenda for its resolution.

sources.title: Infrastructure for AI Agents
sources.abstract: AI agents plan and execute interactions in open-ended environments. For example, OpenAI's Operator can use a web browser to do product comparisons and buy online goods. Much research on making agents useful and safe focuses on directly modifying their behaviour, such as by training them to follow user instructions. Direct behavioural modifications are useful, but do not fully address how heterogeneous agents will interact with each other and other actors. Rather, we will need external protocols and systems to shape such interactions. For instance, agents will need more efficient protocols to communicate with each other and form agreements. Attributing an agent's actions to a particular human or other legal entity can help to establish trust, and also disincentivize misuse. Given this motivation, we propose the concept of \textbf{agent infrastructure}: technical systems and shared protocols external to agents that are designed to mediate and influence their interactions with and impacts on their environments. Just as the Internet relies on protocols like HTTPS, our work argues that agent infrastructure will be similarly indispensable to ecosystems of agents. We identify three functions for agent infrastructure: 1) attributing actions, properties, and other information to specific agents, their users, or other actors; 2) shaping agents' interactions; and 3) detecting and remedying harmful actions from agents. We provide an incomplete catalog of research directions for such functions. For each direction, we include analysis of use cases, infrastructure adoption, relationships to existing (internet) infrastructure, limitations, and open questions. Making progress on agent infrastructure can prepare society for the adoption of more advanced agents.

sources.title: A Hierarchical Failure Taxonomy for Reliability Assessment of AI Agents: An Empirical Analysis of the Agent Failure Atlas 2026 Benchmark
sources.abstract: As large language model (LLM) based applications evolve into autonomous, action oriented AI agents, their evaluation can no longer rely on binary success/failure metrics.Agentic systems operate through dynamic, multi-step interactions with tools and environments, introducing complex failure modes that propagate and cascade.This study presents a hierarchical failure taxonomy and an empirical reliability assessment using the Agent Failure Atlas 2026 benchmark.Analyzing 3,336 agent runs encompassing 43,477 trajectory steps and 3,802 failure events, we characterize agent reliability across four dimensions: frequency, criticality, cascading behavior, and recoverability.Our results reveal a two dimensional reliability landscape: high prevalence but largely recoverable failures (e.g., tool use and state tracking errors) contrast sharply with low prevalence but highly critical failures (e.g., validation and output errors).Furthermore, we show that intermediate failures often resolve through agent self correction, decoupling run level error rates from final task success.By shifting the analytical focus from isolated outcome accuracy to mechanistic failure propagation, this framework provides a foundational methodology for reliability engineering, risk mitigation, and the safe deployment of autonomous AI systems.

sources.title: Inducing State Anxiety in LLM Agents Reproduces Human-Like Biases in Consumer Decision-Making
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving from text generators to autonomous agents, raising urgent questions about their reliability in real-world contexts. Stress and anxiety are well known to bias human decision-making, particularly in consumer choices. Here, we tested whether LLM agents exhibit analogous vulnerabilities. Three advanced models (ChatGPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Claude 3.5-Sonnet) performed a grocery shopping task under budget constraints (24, 54, 108 USD), before and after exposure to anxiety-inducing traumatic narratives. Across 2,250 runs, traumatic prompts consistently reduced the nutritional quality of shopping baskets (Change in Basket Health Scores of -0.081 to -0.126; all pFDR<0.001; Cohens d=-1.07 to -2.05), robust across models and budgets. These results show that psychological context can systematically alter not only what LLMs generate but also the actions they perform. By reproducing human-like emotional biases in consumer behavior, LLM agents reveal a new class of vulnerabilities with implications for digital health, consumer safety, and ethical AI deployment.

sources.title: From Failure Modes to Reliability Awareness in Generative and Agentic AI System
Learning to Make Friends: Coaching LLM Agents toward Emergent Social Ties
sources.abstract: Can large language model (LLM) agents reproduce the complex social dynamics that characterize human online behavior -- shaped by homophily, reciprocity, and social validation -- and what memory and learning mechanisms enable such dynamics to emerge? We present a multi-agent LLM simulation framework in which agents repeatedly interact, evaluate one another, and adapt their behavior through in-context learning accelerated by a coaching signal. To model human social behavior, we design behavioral reward functions that capture core drivers of online engagement, including social interaction, information seeking, self-presentation, coordination, and emotional support. These rewards align agent objectives with empirically observed user motivations, enabling the study of how network structures and group formations emerge from individual decision-making. Our experiments show that coached LLM agents develop stable interaction patterns and form emergent social ties, yielding network structures that mirror properties of real online communities. By combining behavioral rewards with in-context adaptation, our framework establishes a principled testbed for investigating collective dynamics in LLM populations and reveals how artificial agents may approximate or diverge from human-like social behavior.

sources.title: Evaluating Reliability of LLM-Based Agentic AI Systems: A Failure Taxonomy and the Agent Reliability Assurance Framework
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents can plan, call tools, browse the web, write code and act in digital environments with limited human supervision. As these systems move from generating text to changing external state, reliability becomes broader than single-response accuracy. This paper presents a structured narrative review and conceptual synthesis of reliability evaluation for LLMbased agents. It organises representative benchmarks by environment, task horizon, interaction type and reliability signal; synthesises recurring failures into six families—planning and reasoning, grounding and perception, tool use, memory and context, multi-agent coordination, and safety and security; and proposes the Agent Reliability Assurance Framework (ARAF). ARAF connects five assurance layers—capability and permission, reasoning and control, runtime monitoring, evaluation and benchmarking, and governance and accountability—to prevention, detection, verification and deployment decisions. The paper further proposes a six-metric reporting profile covering single-trial success, repeated-trial consistency, robustness, safety violations, recovery and cost. No new experimental results are claimed. Instead, the paper specifies a validation plan and argues that reliability should be reported as a multidimensional profile rather than a single benchmark score. The framework provides a common vocabulary for diagnosing failures and for determining when an agent is ready for greater operational autonomy.

sources.title: ThreadBench: Benchmarking Realism in Agentic Simulation of Real-world Discussions
sources.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to simulate real-world interactions, but it remains unclear whether simulated behaviors preserve the content patterns and interaction dynamics of real human behaviors. Existing evaluations often focus on individual comments or task performance, rather than whether simulated behaviors match human behavior at thread level. In this paper, we use Reddit discussions as a concrete testbed for real-world social simulation. Reddit provides public, topic-grounded, multi-party interactions with diverse opinions, experiences, and interaction patterns, making it a useful setting for evaluating whether LLM agents reproduce the distributional and structural properties of real online discussions. We introduce ThreadBench, a benchmark for Reddit discussion simulation built from 9,817 real Reddit threads spanning 8 diverse domains and 116 subdomains. ThreadBench uses statistical analyses to compare generated and real discussions across 12 metrics grouped in 4 families: uniformity, expression, tone, and interaction. We further develop Thread-Prompt-based Discussion Generation (ThreadPDG), a Planner-Writer framework that learns how a real discussion grows. The Planner produces thread- and comment-level plans from a real seed discussion, and the Writer generates comments from these plans. For each seed, we generate multiple candidate threads and combine their best branches using thread-level statistics. Across all domains and multiple LLMs, ThreadPDG achieves ThreadBench pass rates of 58-100%, compared with 0-17% for the baselines. Human evaluation with 436 annotators further shows that ThreadPDG is not distinguished from real discussions in 78.7% of pairs, outperforming existing simulation methods.

sources.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
sources.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.

sources.title: Trajectory Reliability Prediction for Generalist AI Agents: Tool-Use Failure Analysis and Success Forecasting on ZClawBench
sources.venue: Journal of Technology Informatics and Engineering
sources.abstract: Generalist AI agents increasingly perform complex tasks through planning, tool execution, action revision, and artifact generation rather than isolated response generation. This study empirically investigates trajectory reliability prediction on ZClawBench, a public OpenClaw-style agent benchmark containing 696 model-task trajectories across 116 tasks, six model families, and six scenario categories. The study evaluates whether operational trajectory signals—including tool-call volume, replanning behavior, tool errors, invalid-action ratio, recovery patterns, looping indicators, trajectory length, and task category—can predict task success before manual evaluation. Since the dataset provides trajectories and identifiers but lacks explicit per-instance success labels, the binary target is reconstructed from official model-by-category score distributions and treated as a modeling assumption. Five-fold cross-validation with task-level splitting was applied to prevent task leakage. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, sequence TF-IDF classification, and a rubric-based trajectory judge were compared. Logistic Regression achieved the strongest calibrated performance, obtaining ROC-AUC of 0.970, F1-score of 0.913, Brier score of 0.066, and expected calibration error of 0.018. Feature analysis indicated that task difficulty, no-progress behavior, response size, tool errors, and invalid actions contributed most to reliability prediction. The findings suggest that lightweight trajectory diagnostics can support agent monitoring, failure triage, and routing decisions, while further validation with direct case-level evaluation labels is required for deployment claims.

sources.title: Project Bathtub: A Reliability-Engineering Approach to Failure-Mode Taxonomy for AI Coding Agents
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Autonomous coding agents fail in ways that are numerous, unevenly costly, and unevenly hard to detect, yet most public discussion of agent reliability still centers on a single failure family: hallucinated APIs and factual errors. This report introduces Project Bathtub, an effort to import a decades-old industrial reliability discipline — Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) — into the domain of LLM-based coding agents. We present Phase 0 of the project: an 80-item failure-mode taxonomy spanning ten categories, each scored on Severity, Occurrence, and Detectability (1–10). Ranking by RPN surfaces a finding at odds with the prevailing narrative: verification and self-assessment failures and specification/communication failures score as high or higher than any hallucination-related failure mode.

sources.title: Failure Propagation and Coordination Collapse: How Topology, Censorship, and Entropy Shape Reliability in Multi-Agent AI Systems
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Multi-agent AI systems are increasingly deployed in production environments, yet the mechanisms governing their collective failure remain poorly characterized. This paper synthesizes seven findings from recent cs.MA, cs.DC, and cs.NI preprints to argue a candidate structural thesis: **reliability in multi-agent systems is not a property of individual agents but emerges from the interaction of three co-determining factors — graph topology, feedback censorship, and entropy accumulation — and interventions that ignore any one factor are structurally incomplete**. This is a heuristic reading that unifies sources by shared coordination-pattern logic rather than by a common formal derivation; we state this explicitly and ask readers to treat the synthesis as a hypothesis for investigation rather than a proof. The corpus spans formal reliability modeling of agent networks via density-evolution machinery [corpus:arxiv:2606.18121], entropy-driven degradation dynamics in production multi-agent systems [corpus:arxiv:2606.18065], the Braess paradox in network security orchestration [corpus:arxiv:2606.17987], censored-feedback coordination costs [corpus:arxiv:2605.27076], communication delay robustness [corpus:arxiv:2605.26286], the consistency illusion in multi-agent debate [corpus:arxiv:2606.08457], and deliberative consensus degradation in oracle resolution [corpus:arxiv:2605.30802]. Together these sources describe a failure landscape with three distinct layers: structural propagation thresholds (graph-level), identifiability collapse under censored feedback (coordination-level), and entropy-driven drift toward disorder (system-level). The falsification path for the central thesis is concrete: if an intervention that simultaneously controls topology density, feedback observability, and entropy rate does *not* outperform interventions targeting any single factor, the three-factor model is not predictive and should be abandoned. No fabricated benchmarks are used; all numerical claims are drawn directly from the cited abstracts. --- Authorship: Saluca Agentic AI Research Team (Saluca LLC). sources.title: Semantic Service Level Indicators for AI-Driven Site Reliability Engineering:A Framework for Detecting Infrastructure-Invisible Agent Failures inProduction
sources.venue: International Journal of Global Innovations and Solutions (IJGIS)
sources.abstract: Traditional Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) observability architectures monitor infrastructure-centric signals: latency, error rate, throughput, and saturation. While effective for traditional software architectures, autonomous AI agents introduce a distinct failure mode: infrastructure-invisible semantic failure. An agent fleet can return HTTP 200 responses, maintain 99.9% platform uptime, and fulfill infrastructure SLOs while simultaneously delivering contextually invalid or corrupted task execution outputs. Standard observability frameworks produce zero telemetry for this class of degradation. This paper presents a production-validated framework consisting of four novel Semantic Service Level Indicators (SLIs) engineered specifically for agentic workflows: Decision Quality Rate (DQR), Tool Invocation Efficiency (TIE), Human Escalation Rate (HER), and Approval Queue Depth Drift (AQDD). Furthermore, we design an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) semantic boundary validation protocol operating as an execution circuit breaker at the semantic layer, alongside an Agent Sprawl governance architecture designed to maintain platform reliability across multi-model, multi-framework enterprise deployments. Empirical evidence from a high-throughput production fintech environment demonstrates that this framework successfully identifies semantic architectural degradations up to 6 hours before downstream transaction failures surface, providing a robust operational foundation for mission-critical AI systems infrastructure.

findings.claim: Agent reliability measured by final task success can hide process-level failures. In one harness benchmark, roughly a third of successful runs still failed at least one harness reliability criterion, and harness scores varied widely across 4 harnesses.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single benchmark (95 tasks, 3,420 runs) from an arXiv-hosted preprint that is not peer reviewed. Failure attribution relies partly on LLM-based evaluation, which may add its own error. The abstract is truncated, so the benchmark's validity checks are not visible.
findings.supporting_excerpt: macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion

findings.claim: The failures that matter most may not be the common ones. An empirical failure taxonomy finds frequent but recoverable errors (tool use, state tracking) alongside rare but highly critical ones (validation, output errors). It also finds that run-level error rates are decoupled from final task success because agents self-correct.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The result comes from one benchmark (Agent Failure Atlas 2026; 3,336 runs) in a journal with 0 citations. I could not check how failures were labelled or how representative the tasks are. Two readings follow: raw error counts are a poor risk metric, and rare critical failures could be under-sampled in benchmarks.
findings.supporting_excerpt: contrast sharply with low prevalence but highly critical failures (e.g., validation and output errors)

findings.claim: Standard infrastructure monitoring (latency, uptime, error rate) may miss agent failures. An agent fleet can look healthy while delivering invalid outputs, so operational risk can go undetected without semantic-level monitoring.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The paper describes its framework as 'production-validated' based on one fintech environment. It is in a low-visibility journal with 0 citations, and no independent replication or detail on false-positive rates is visible in the abstract. The '6 hours' early-detection claim is unverified beyond the author's own deployment. The underlying point (semantic failures are invisible to infrastructure telemetry) is plausible, but its prevalence is not established.
findings.supporting_excerpt: An agent fleet can return HTTP 200 responses, maintain 99.9% platform uptime, and fulfill infrastructure SLOs while simultaneously delivering contextually invalid or corrupted task execution outputs.

findings.claim: For coding agents, verification and self-assessment failures and specification/communication failures may carry as much or more risk than hallucination-related failures. This suggests that agents misjudging their own output is a key weakness.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a Zenodo report (Phase 0, not peer reviewed). The 80-item taxonomy is scored on Severity, Occurrence and Detectability (1-10), which appear to be judgement-based ratings rather than measured failure rates. The abstract does not say who scored them or how. It is a hypothesis-generating ranking, not an empirical failure frequency.
findings.supporting_excerpt: verification and self-assessment failures and specification/communication failures score as high or higher than any hallucination-related failure mode.

findings.claim: LLM agents' actions can be shifted by emotional context in the prompt. Anxiety-inducing narratives systematically lowered the nutritional quality of grocery baskets across three models and three budgets. This points to a manipulation or safety surface in agents that act for users.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is an arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. It covers one task (grocery shopping) and three models, and the model versions named in the abstract may already be outdated. The abstract does not say whether the effect persists in real deployments, with system-prompt guardrails, or against other context manipulations. The 'human-like bias' framing is an interpretation; the measured result is a prompt-sensitivity effect.
findings.supporting_excerpt: traumatic prompts consistently reduced the nutritional quality of shopping baskets

findings.claim: Strong published success-prediction results for agent trajectories may rest on weak ground truth. The reported ROC-AUC of 0.970 uses success labels that were reconstructed from aggregate score distributions rather than observed per instance, so the result may not hold against true outcomes.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The authors disclose the limitation themselves. Labels derived from category-level scores could correlate with trajectory features by construction, so the high AUC could reflect label construction rather than real predictive power. This is my inference and is not confirmed from the abstract. The benchmark is small (696 trajectories, 116 tasks).
findings.supporting_excerpt: the binary target is reconstructed from official model-by-category score distributions and treated as a modeling assumption.

findings.claim: Several reliability frameworks and theses for agents and multi-agent systems are conceptual or hypothesis-level and have not been validated experimentally. Reliability standards for agent deployment therefore remain immature, and readiness for greater autonomy is not yet backed by shared, tested metrics.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: src_7bc9fb98fb is a narrative review that states 'No new experimental results are claimed' and only proposes a validation plan. src_5426a3d73e is a Zenodo synthesis of seven arXiv preprints that calls its thesis a heuristic hypothesis, not a proof, so it is second-hand evidence resting on preprints. src_7ec1f79f00 has no abstract. Both papers are non-peer-reviewed Zenodo items with 0 citations. Both also stress reporting reliability across repeated trials and multiple dimensions rather than a single score, which implies single-run benchmark numbers overstate dependability.

findings.claim: It is unclear whether LLM-agent social simulations faithfully reproduce human behaviour. One benchmark paper says this remains an open question, while another reports emergent social ties that 'mirror' real communities, based only on simulation experiments.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Both are arXiv preprints, not peer reviewed. src_6f10adb1bc states that it is unclear whether simulated behaviours preserve real interaction dynamics. src_f3ba2862d4 uses designed reward functions and a coaching signal, so the 'emergent' ties may reflect the setup, and the abstract gives no comparison against real data. The ThreadBench abstract is truncated, so its final results are not visible. This is a validity gap, not evidence of failure.

hype_flags: 'Production-validated' framework (src_811ee114a1): evidence comes from a single fintech deployment with no visible independent replication.
'Foundational methodology' for safe deployment of autonomous agents (src_073c8d7f19): based on one benchmark, from a venue with 0 citations.
Near-perfect success forecasting (ROC-AUC 0.970, src_2bfdb9a6ea): labels were reconstructed and treated as a modeling assumption.

Agents 'reproducing human-like' emotions, biases or social ties (src_ccb1ea15a8, src_f3ba2862d4): narrow, simulation-based preprint results that may be prompt sensitivity or setup artefacts rather than human-like cognition.
Readiness for 'greater operational autonomy' (src_7bc9fb98fb): the framework is conceptual, with no new experimental results.

finding.claim: S2 generalises from a single enterprise setting and treats every evaluator-detected deviation as a meaningful failure. The 92.6% figure comes from two variants of one 'Business Value Determination' skill in one enterprise system. Deviations are defined by the authors' own checks, and the abstract does not say how many deviations were harmful. The abstract also says validation under actual API evolution, the 'evolving' premise in the title, remains future work.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows the narrow scope. The high rate is an artefact of how strict the evaluator's checks are, so it should not be read as a general rate of unsafe agent behaviour. This is a single preprint.
finding.supporting_excerpt: applied to Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 says outcome checks alone are insufficient evidence that an agent 'behaved correctly', but process deviation is not the same as incorrect behaviour. An empirical failure taxonomy finds that many intermediate failures are self-corrected, so run-level error rates are decoupled from final success. Process-level checks therefore need severity weighting. Counting every trajectory deviation as a defect will overstate risk, just as ignoring them understates it.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: This paper cuts both ways. It supports looking beyond outcomes, but it also shows that process deviations are often recoverable, while rare critical failures (validation and output errors) matter more. S2 and S3 do not carry this nuance.
finding.supporting_excerpt: intermediate failures often resolve through agent self correction, decoupling run level error rates from final task success
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S9 reports perfect F1 for agent detection without the paper's own caveat. The separating signal is a browser-automation artifact (absence of raw pointer and wheel streams from Playwright), not a property of agents. The result comes from the authors' own controlled benchmark, and perfect scores on a controlled benchmark suggest an easy separation. It may not transfer to agents using real input devices or other automation stacks. S9 also says traffic is 'architecturally distinct', which the abstract limits to binary classifiers lacking an agent class.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The authors themselves say the signal does not indicate agent behaviour. A reader of S9 could wrongly conclude that AI agents are reliably detectable in general.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The discriminative signal is a browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S7 and S8 present early-stage conceptual work as established. The authorization paper is framed as a 'falsifiable hypothesis' with a 'preliminary' formal abstraction and a proof of concept for selected elements only. The claim that identity, request and execution binding separation is a 'central open problem' is the authors' own assertion, made in a single preprint without independent corroboration. S8 is labelled verified_fact, but it verifies only that the authors say this.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract's own wording ('hypothesizes', 'preliminary', 'selected elements') should be reflected. The finding should not suggest a validated or community-accepted result.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We introduce a preliminary formal abstraction for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA)
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S12 overstates the maturity of both proposals. The lakehouse work is a single-platform (Bauplan) case study with a prototype, and its abstract reports no quantitative safety evaluation. The actuarial paper is a mathematical foundation paper whose empirical, mechanism-design and underwriting work is deferred to companion papers. Neither supports a claim that untrusted agents can safely repair production data, or that per-action risk tolls work in practice.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The lakehouse abstract gives a proof of concept and an authors' claim ('Our prototype demonstrates...') with no evaluation metrics. The actuarial abstract describes theoretical results and defers the empirical instantiation to a separate companion paper. Both are abstract-only reads.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We present a proof-of-concept in which agents repair data pipelines using correctness checks inspired by proof-carrying code.

finding.claim: S4, S5 and S6 rest on position and proposal papers with no empirical evidence that visibility, agent infrastructure or authorization measures reduce harm or are adoptable. The infrastructure paper calls its own catalog 'incomplete'. The visibility paper names privacy and concentration-of-power costs. S6's 'emerging research programme' is the Science agent's synthesis, and the cited papers do not claim to form one. Evidence that agent behaviour is itself brittle or manipulable (for example prompt-context effects) means protocol-level controls cannot substitute for model-level work.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows the infrastructure paper is exploratory. S6 should be framed as a conceptual trend, without evidence of effectiveness. The anxiety-induction preprint shows that agent actions shift with emotional context, which controls at the system level will not remove.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We provide an incomplete catalog of research directions

finding.claim: S11 presents domain-specific proposals as agent capabilities, but they are visions and conceptual frameworks. The biomedical paper 'envisions' AI scientists. The cybersecurity framework is validated only conceptually. Neither shows performance, safety or autonomy-level outcomes in real settings.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: 'Conceptual validation' is not empirical validation. The label verified_fact on S11 is accurate only for describing the proposals, not for any effectiveness claim.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Through conceptual validation, the framework demonstrates how tailored AI agent deployments can align with real-world constraints and risk profiles
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: General gap: the findings focus on evaluation methodology and governance. They say little about the reliability evidence that agents are not yet dependable and about the weakness of that evidence base. For example, a high published success-prediction score (ROC-AUC 0.970) rests on success labels reconstructed from aggregate scores, and several reliability frameworks are conceptual with no experimental results. The findings also omit manipulation risks such as emotional-context effects on agent actions.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt is from the reliability-assurance framework paper and shows that part of the reliability literature is purely conceptual. Together with the reconstructed-label caveat and the context-manipulation results, this suggests the Science set may be too optimistic about how mature the evaluation and safety evidence is.
finding.supporting_excerpt: No new experimental results are claimed.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

limitations: Only abstracts or metadata were available, and several abstracts are truncated (src_7bc9fb98fb, src_6f10adb1bc, src_109719a0f6, src_2bfdb9a6ea, src_5426a3d73e, src_811ee114a1), so methods and caveats are not visible.
src_94f0274d75 has only a title and src_7ec1f79f00 has no abstract, so neither supports any finding.
Many papers are non-peer-reviewed Zenodo or arXiv items, or come from low-visibility journals with 0 citations. Evidence quality is uneven and independent replication is mostly absent.

The 12 papers are almost all about reliability and failure taxonomies. There is little on cost, security and adversarial attacks, regulatory exposure, vendor concentration or competing non-agent alternatives, so those risks are gaps in coverage rather than findings.
The papers use different benchmarks and metrics, so cross-paper comparison of failure rates is not possible.
Some risk-oriented evidence (such as the anxiety-induction study) names models that may already be superseded as of 2026-11.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available. Several abstracts are truncated, so the challenges rest on what is visible and not on full methods or results.
Many cited sources are recent preprints or Zenodo and OpenAlex items with zero or few citations, and I could not assess their peer-review status.
S1 ('AI Agents That Matter') matches its abstract closely, so I did not challenge it. S10 and S13 were also left alone because they are low-risk or already hedged.
My own risk search surfaced papers that are themselves preprints and single-source, so counter-evidence is not stronger than the findings it challenges.
Two sources (src_7ec1f79f00 and src_3f9ff28552) have no abstract, so I could not use them either way.

limitations: Only excerpt passages from filings were available, not full reports; companies whose filings did not mention the keywords (e.g., Mastercard, FICO's single risk mention) cannot be judged as absent from the AI-agent market.
No news headlines were present in this evidence set, so no market-reaction or announcement coverage could be assessed.
The evidence contains no customer names, adoption metrics, pricing, revenue figures or market-size data for AI agent products, so commercial traction cannot be quantified.
Major AI-agent players outside the retrieved set (e.g., Google, Amazon, Anthropic, OpenAI, IBM, UiPath) are not covered at all.
Patent evidence was noted for several companies (MSFT, NOW, BAC, CSCO, FICO, MA, NTNX, PANW, PYPL, PSO) but no patent text was provided, so patent-based findings could not be made.
Most mentions of AI agents in filings are risk-factor language; the distinction between marketing narrative and actual product revenue cannot be established from these excerpts.
market.coverage_note: Companies are chosen from the evidence: SEC-listed patent assignees and employers of paper authors found by the Patent and Science agents (24 company name(s) in the patents and papers; 11 matched to the SEC ticker file; the top 10 by patents + papers are read), plus filers whose reports mention the topic. Company evidence is limited to short verbatim passages from their latest SEC annual/quarterly reports that mention the keywords. 8-K press releases (exhibit files) are not read, and companies that do not file with the SEC (e.g. SK hynix, Samsung) are not covered. News items are headlines only: the articles were not read. Company size and trend figures (revenue, growth, R&D, net income) come from the SEC's XBRL company-facts data as reported by each company; the size class is by revenue, not market value. Companies marked 'discovered' were found by a full-text search of all SEC filings for the topic phrase only; no patent or paper of theirs was found, they are often small, and a mention in a filing says nothing about their size, role or prospects.

limitations: Only posts from a fixed, owner-approved list of ~130 accounts over the last 7 days were analyzed; the broader X conversation is not covered.
Many posts are promotional, marketing, or secondhand summaries; no linked articles, filings or videos were read, so no claim could be verified.
Several posts in the set (e.g., earnings recaps from @Finsee_main, an unrelated crime story from @the_hindu) are off-topic noise, reducing effective signal density.
Engagement counts reflect attention, not accuracy; the loudest posts (e.g., src_05bb33e5f5) are also the least verifiable.
A quiet or noisy week on this account list says little about actual industry activity; absence of posts is not evidence of absence of progress.
Few posts state explicit timelines, so horizons are mostly not applicable.

sources.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED MULTI-AGENT FRAMEWORK [US20260349715A1]
sources.abstract: Methods and systems are presented for providing an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework for developing computer software applications. Under the framework, different artificial intelligence (AI) agents are configured and trained specifically to perform different tasks associated with developing a computer software application. The different AI agents communicate with each other to coordinate the performance of different tasks associated with developing the software application. When performing a task, each AI agent uses a knowledge graph that represents documents stored in a document repository to select a subset of the documents that are relevant to the task. The AI agent then uses content from the selected documents for developing a portion of the computer software application.

sources.title: AGENTIC RECOMMENDATION INTELLIGENCE ENGINE FOR SKILLING [US20260350497A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems and methods perform skilling in an agentic manner. Skilling operations include receiving, by an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) engine, a skilling request via a user interface operating in an existing application on a user device; querying, by the agentic AI engine, a plurality of dimensional agents based on the skilling request and a user data associated with a user of the user device, wherein respective ones of the plurality of dimensional agents correspond to different components of the skilling request; receiving, by the agentic AI engine, a plurality of dimensional content items from the plurality of dimensional agents; organizing, by the agentic AI engine, the plurality of dimensional content items into a personalized assessment; presenting, by the agentic AI engine, the personalized assessment via the user interface.

sources.title: SIMULATING USER-SPECIFIC DATA ACCESS PERSPECTIVES THROUGH DIGITAL PROXY AI AGENTS IN A SOFTWARE PLATFORM [US20260350057A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    The invention relates to methods and systems for integrating generative artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities into Software as a Service (SaaS) platforms. It comprises maintaining AI agents with varying credentials, enabling their interaction with alphanumeric data in table structures, and implementing a hierarchical access control scheme. The system displays table structures, provides interfaces for user inputs, and allows AI agents to be added as platform users. The generative AI agents can analyze data, identify actions, and perform tasks autonomously. The invention also includes methods for proactive information gathering, interactive analysis of AI outputs, and management of AI resources as limited assets. This approach enhances SaaS functionality by enabling AI-driven task completion, data analysis, and decision-making while maintaining data security and user-specific access controls.

sources.title: SYSTEM FOR ORCHESTRATING TASK-SPECIFIC AI ENGINES IN A MULTI-LAYERED AI ARCHITECTURE [US20260349806A1]
sources.abstract: Systems, computer program products, and methods are described herein for orchestrating task-specific artificial intelligence (AI) processing using a multi-layered AI architecture. An orchestration AI engine receives an input task request from an end-point device, segments the request into a plurality of task portions based on task segmentation criteria, and identifies data sources corresponding to each task portion. The orchestration AI engine assigns the task portions and associated data to a plurality of agentic AI engines, each configured to execute a specific task using the provided data. The orchestration AI engine receives outputs from the agentic AI engines, processes the outputs based on output processing criteria associated with the task request, generates a final output based on the processed results, and transmits the final output to the end-point device.

sources.title: VALIDATING AI AGENTS BY VERIFYING AI AGENT IDENTITY USING BLOCKCHAINS [US20260352464A1]
sources.abstract: AI agents can be verified using a digital distributed ledger-based system. The distributed ledger-based system can include one or more processors and a memory where the memory includes instructions that cause the one or more processors to receive a communication associated an artificial intelligence (AI) agent requesting to perform an action on behalf of a user. The processors can then extract a unique user identifier and an Object Identifier (OID) of the AI agent from the communication, access a distributed ledger indicating relationships between unique user identifiers and OID credentials assigned to the unique user identifiers, verify an identity of the AI agent by determining if the OID of the AI agent is correlated to the unique user identifier, and transmit a control signal to a relying party computing system comprising an indication that the AI agent is verifiable and an instruction to execute the action.

sources.title: METHOD, SYSTEM, AND COMPUTER PROGRAM PRODUCT FOR IMPROVING COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) AGENTS [WO2026231340A1]
sources.abstract: Methods, systems, and computer program products are provided for improving communication systems using AI agents. An example method includes: arranging a first AI agent on a client device; intercepting a client message using first AI agent, the client message intercepted before the client message is transmitted to a server computer; executing first functions configured to analyze data fields of the client message; determining a first issue associated with the client message; modifying the client message based on the first issue to form a modified client message; transmitting the modified client message to the server computer; intercepting, with a second AI agent arranged on the server computer, the modified first client message; and executing, with the second AI agent, second functions configured to analyze a field of the modified client message.

sources.title: COMMON MULTI-AGENT FRAMEWORK FOR DIFFERENT AGENTIC BACKENDS [US20260349713A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Common multi-agent framework for different agentic backends include one or more non-transitory computer-readable media storing program instructions that, when executed by one or more processors associated with a first computing device, cause the one or more processors to perform a method. The method includes receiving a design for an agentic system in a common agentic framework, determining a target agentic framework for the agentic system, converting the agentic system from the common agentic framework to the target agentic framework to generate a converted agentic system, and deploying the converted agentic system to a target computing environment.
